etymology: From Old English cene (bold, brave, fierce), a Germanic word. The older English senses — sharp-edged, eager, piercing ("a keen wind") — are centuries old and are those Webster gave in 1828. The slang sense — attractive, excellent, first-rate — is American and was in wide use by the 1930s and 1940s; the rhyming peachy keen belongs to the late 1940s and 1950s and was a schoolyard favorite of the Silent Generation.
biblical_def: In 1946 a girl who said a new dress was keen meant it was sharp, smart, first-rate — and if it was really something, it was peachy keen. Your grandmother may still say it. The word is older than the slang, and the older meaning is the better one: in 1828 keen meant sharp-edged, eager, piercing. A keen blade cuts clean. Scripture has a good deal to say about sharpness. "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Pro 27:17) — a true friend keeps your edge keen by honest talk. God wants His people keen in the old sense: "Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord" (Rom 12:11). And the keenest edge in the world is His Word, which is "sharper than any twoedged sword … a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart" (Heb 4:12). That blade cuts us before it heals us; it shows us our sin and then shows us Christ, who was pierced for it. So when Grandpa says something is keen, let it remind you to be keen yourself — eager for the things of God, sharp in your thinking, quick to think on "whatsoever things are lovely" (Php 4:8). The slang praises what looks sharp. The Word of God makes you sharp.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (American, 1930s–50s; "peachy keen") for sharp, attractive, first-rate — grown from the 1828 sense of sharp-edged and eager, which Scripture commends in the friend who sharpens his friend (Pro 27:17).
webster_full: KEEN, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; American from the 1930s) Attractive, excellent, first-rate. "That’s a keen sweater." Also peachy keen.

Webster (1828) — KEEN, adjective 1. Eager; vehement; as hungry curs too keen at the sport. 2. Eager; sharp; as a keen appetite. 3. Sharp; having a very fine edge; as a keen razor, or a razor with a keen edge. We say a keen edge, but a sharp point. 4. Piercing; penetrating; severe; applied to cold or to wind; as a keen wind; the cold is very keen
Decode for families: peachy keen means terrific; the old keen means sharp and eager — be both for the Lord.
scriptures: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word; the only loss is that the slang "looks sharp" has crowded out the older "is sharp" — eager, keen-edged, alert — which Scripture asks of every believer.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in keen. It is one of the cleanest compliments the 1940s produced, and a grandmother who calls a granddaughter’s drawing peachy keen is doing something kind. The only thing lost is depth: the slang praises how a thing looks, while the old word named what a thing is — sharp, eager, ready.

A Christian family can keep both senses. Praise what is keen in the slang way, and pray to be keen in the old way: eager for the Word, sharpened by honest friends (Pro 27:17), fervent in spirit (Rom 12:11), and cut to the heart by the sharpest blade there is (Heb 4:12).
roots_summary: Old English cene (bold, fierce) → English keen (sharp, eager, piercing) → American slang (attractive, excellent) → 1940s–50s peachy keen.
roots_lines: Old English cene — bold, brave, fierce
Middle English kene — sharp, eager, bitter
1828 Webster: keen — eager; sharp-edged; piercing
1930s–40s American slang: keen — attractive, excellent
Late 1940s–50s: peachy keen — the Silent Generation’s rhyming superlative
usage: "Grandma held up my report card and said, ‘Well, isn’t that peachy keen.’ I knew I was in good shape."
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend (Pro 27:17).
Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord (Rom 12:11).

etymology: From hep (in the know, up to date), American slang recorded from the early 1900s and of uncertain origin, plus cat, the jazz musicians’ word for a fellow, especially one who loved swing. Hep cat appears in Cab Calloway’s Hepster’s Dictionary (1938) for a guy who knows all the answers and understands jive. By the 1950s hep was giving way to hip, and the hepcat to the hipster.
biblical_def: A hepcat in 1941 was the young fellow at the dance hall who knew every record on the jukebox, wore his trousers just so, and could tell you which band was hot and which was corny. To be hep was to be in the know. There is nothing wrong with loving good music; David was the sweetest musician in Israel, and the psalm says to "play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3). The trouble with being hep is the thing it prizes: knowing what the crowd knows a little before the crowd knows it. That kind of knowledge goes stale by next summer, and it tempts a man to look down on the fellow who is not in on it. "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1). God warns us, "Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil" (Pro 3:7), and He reminds us that "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The Christian is called to be "not conformed to this world" (Rom 12:2) — and being hep is only conformity that runs a step ahead of the crowd. The one knowledge worth being in on is the knowledge of Christ, which never goes out of style and which He gives freely to the plainest square in the room. A grandfather who was a hepcat at seventeen can tell you: the records changed, the suits changed, the slang changed. The Lord did not.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (late 1930s–40s swing era) for a stylish young man in the know about jazz and jive — a word that prized being ahead of the crowd, where Scripture prizes a heart the LORD looks upon (1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: HEPCAT, n. (Silent Generation slang, late 1930s–40s; swing era) A jazz-loving, stylish young man; one who is hep, in the know. "Every hepcat in town turned out for the band." Later hipster.
Decode for families: a hepcat was the cool kid of 1941 — Grandpa’s word for what you would call being in the know.
scriptures: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
corruption_summary: Mostly harmless; the snare in being hep is pride in insider knowledge and contempt for the "square" who is not in on it.
corruption_paragraphs: A love of music and a sharp suit are no sin, and most hepcats of 1941 were simply boys having fun before the war took them. The word itself is innocent. What it celebrates is the small thrill of being ahead of the crowd, and that thrill has a shadow: the habit of sorting people into those who get it and those who do not.

Scripture names that shadow plainly. Knowledge that puffs up is not the knowledge God values (1Co 8:1), and being wise in one’s own eyes is the opposite of fearing the LORD (Pro 3:7). A Christian can enjoy the music and still refuse the contempt, because the One who matters looks on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
roots_summary: American hep (in the know, early 1900s) + jazz cat (a fellow) → hep cat (1938, swing slang) → hepcat (1940s) → hip, hipster (1950s).
roots_lines: Early 1900s American: hep — aware, up to date; origin uncertain
1920s–30s jazz: cat — a fellow, a swing fan or musician
1938: hep cat in Cab Calloway’s Hepster’s Dictionary
1940s: hepcat — the stylish, jive-talking swing fan
1950s: hip, hipster replace the older forms
usage: "Your grandfather was a real hepcat in ’41 — two-tone shoes and every Glenn Miller record."
Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1).
Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil (Pro 3:7).

etymology: A 1950s jazz and beatnik intensifier of square (a conventional, unhip person, recorded from the 1940s): if a square is dull in two dimensions, a cube is square in three. Recorded in 1950s slang; of no known coiner. The noun itself is from Greek kubos, a die, through Latin cubus, and in its geometric sense it is the word Webster defined in 1828.
biblical_def: In 1957 a square was a fellow who did not get it — did not dig the music, kept his hair short, went to church, minded his parents. A cube was squarer still: square on every side. It was a joke, and a sneering one. Here is something the beatniks did not know: the holiest room on earth was a cube. The inner sanctuary of Solomon’s temple, where the ark rested, was "twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in the height thereof" (1Ki 6:20). And when John saw the New Jerusalem, "The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal" (Rev 21:16). The place where God dwells with His people is a perfect cube. So the Christian may wear the insult with a smile. The world has always thought it odd when believers would not join in: "they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you" (1Pe 4:4). But "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise" (1Co 1:27), and the Lord still says, "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls" (Jer 6:16). Being square for its own sake is no virtue; a stiff, proud squareness is its own kind of pride. But being plumb, level, and true — built to the measure God gives — is what a cube is. Christ was the one perfectly upright man, and the hip crowd of His day crucified Him for it.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s jazz and beatnik talk) for a person even squarer than a square — though the holiest room of the temple and the New Jerusalem itself are perfect cubes, equal on every side (Rev 21:16).
webster_full: CUBE, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beatnik talk) A hopelessly conventional person; worse than a square. "Don’t invite him — he’s a real cube."

Webster (1828) — CUBE, noun [Gr., Latin , a die or cube; to set or throw down, that which is set or laid, a solid mass.] 1. In geometry, a regular solid body, with six equal sides, and containing equal angles.
Decode for families: a square was dull; a cube was dull on every side — yet God built His holy of holies as a cube.
scriptures: And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal.

And the oracle in the forepart was twenty cubits in length, and twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in the height thereof: and he overlaid it with pure gold; and so covered the altar which was of cedar.
Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
corruption_summary: A word of contempt for the conventional; its sin is mockery of the plain and the upright, though a believer should not mistake mere stiffness for godliness either.
corruption_paragraphs: Cube was coined to sneer. It mocked the boy who did his homework, the girl who kept her curfew, the family that went to church on Sunday. Scripture warns that the scorner is no friend of wisdom, and it tells believers to expect such talk: the world thinks it strange when Christians will not run with it (1Pe 4:4).

There is a second, gentler warning. Not every square is righteous. A man can be conventional out of fear, stiff out of pride, and plain because he never thought about it. The Christian’s squareness is meant to be the uprightness of a life built to God’s measure, like the holy of holies (1Ki 6:20) — not a badge to wear against the hip crowd.
roots_summary: Greek kubos (a die) → Latin cubus → English cube (six equal sides) → 1940s square (conventional person) → 1950s cube (squarer than square).
roots_lines: Greek kubos — a die for gaming; a cube
Latin cubus → French and English cube
1828 Webster: cube — a solid with six equal sides
1940s jazz slang: square — an unhip, conventional person
1950s beatnik slang: cube — square in three dimensions
usage: "The kids at the coffeehouse called me a cube because I had to be home by ten. I was home by ten."
The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal (Rev 21:16).
Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths (Jer 6:16).

etymology: From jitters (nervous shaking), American slang recorded from the 1920s and of uncertain origin, plus bug (an enthusiast, someone crazy for a thing). Cab Calloway’s 1934 recording "Call of the Jitter Bug" spread the word; by the late 1930s jitterbug named both the swing dancer and the athletic dance itself, and in the war years American servicemen carried it around the world.
biblical_def: When your grandparents were young, the jitterbug was the dance. A boy would swing a girl out, pull her back, sometimes toss her right over his shoulder, while a big band played as fast as it could. The name poked fun at it: the dancers looked as if they had the jitters. Is dancing wrong? Scripture says it has its time: "a time to mourn, and a time to dance" (Ecc 3:4). Israel was told, "Let them praise his name in the dance" (Psa 149:3), and when the ark came home to Jerusalem, "David danced before the LORD with all his might" (2Sa 6:14). Joy that moves the feet is a gift from God. But dancing is like every gift: it can be used for Him or against Him. The same Bible tells of a girl who danced before Herod, and a prophet lost his head for it. Christian young people of the 1940s were taught to keep the dance floor clean — for young women to dress "in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety" (1Ti 2:9) and for young men to keep their hands and thoughts where they belonged. And there is the other half of the word: the jitters. The war years were full of them — a brother overseas, a telegram that might come. The cure for the jitters is not a faster song but a Father who hears: "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God" (Php 4:6). Christ calms the storm in the heart, and then the feet can dance.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1930s–40s swing era) for the fast, acrobatic swing dance and the dancer who loved it — joy in motion, which Scripture allows its time (Ecc 3:4) and governs with modesty and sobriety (1Ti 2:9).
webster_full: JITTERBUG, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1930s–40s; swing era) 1. A fast, acrobatic swing dance. 2. One who dances it with enthusiasm. "They jitterbugged till the band packed up." Also as a verb.
Decode for families: the jitterbug was Grandma and Grandpa’s big dance; the jitters are the nerves — prayer is the cure for those.
scriptures: A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
Let them praise his name in the dance: let them sing praises unto him with the timbrel and harp.
And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
corruption_summary: A wholesome word for a joyful dance; the cautions Scripture brings are modesty on the dance floor and trust in God instead of the jitters.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wicked in the word or in the joy behind it. The jitterbug was mostly young people letting off steam in hard years, and Scripture gives dancing its place (Ecc 3:4; Psa 149:3). The caution is the one that attends every close and lively dance: a dance floor can be an innocent place or a careless one, and modesty and sobriety are the difference (1Ti 2:9).

The name also carries the word jitters, and it is worth teaching children what to do with those. Nervous fear is not answered by noise but by prayer with thanksgiving (Php 4:6). The generation that danced the jitterbug also knelt in a great many churches between 1941 and 1945.
roots_summary: American jitters (nervous shaking, 1920s) + bug (an enthusiast) → 1934 "Call of the Jitter Bug" → late 1930s jitterbug (the dance and the dancer) → worldwide in WWII.
roots_lines: 1920s American slang: the jitters — nervous shaking; origin uncertain
American bug — an enthusiast, one crazy for something
1934: Cab Calloway’s "Call of the Jitter Bug"
Late 1930s: jitterbug — the swing dancer and the dance
1940s: carried abroad by American servicemen
usage: "Grandma says she could jitterbug all night at the USO and still make the first shift at the plant."
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance (Ecc 3:4).
Let them praise his name in the dance (Psa 149:3).

etymology: American swing slang, recorded from the late 1930s: killer (something overwhelmingly good) doubled with the rhyming diller. Swing fans used it for a hot number, a terrific band, or anything first-rate, and it stayed in use through the 1940s. Of no known coiner.
biblical_def: To a swing fan of 1940, a killer-diller was the best: a band that really jumped, a new record, a smart car. It is a cheerful word, and nobody using it was thinking of death. But it is worth noticing that the slang of every generation borrows the language of killing to praise things — a killer band, it slays me, you killed it. Words matter more than we think. "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Pro 18:21). God gave the commandment "Thou shalt not kill" (Exo 20:13) because human life bears His image, and the men of that generation learned what killing really was; many came home from it and never joked about it again. The Christian need not scold a grandfather for calling a band a killer-diller. But he can choose words that "minister grace unto the hearers" (Eph 4:29), remembering that "every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof" (Mat 12:36). And the Christian knows the one true killer-diller: the death of Christ, which put death itself to death. "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (1Co 15:55). That is the most sensational, first-rate news there ever was, and it is no slang.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (late 1930s–40s swing era) for anything sensational or first-rate — a cheerful word that borrows the language of killing, and a reminder that death and life are in the power of the tongue (Pro 18:21).
webster_full: KILLER-DILLER, n. (Silent Generation slang, late 1930s–40s; swing era) Something or someone sensational, first-rate. "That new band is a killer-diller."
Decode for families: killer-diller meant terrific; nobody meant killing — but it is good to notice how often we borrow death to praise things.
scriptures: Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof.
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
corruption_summary: A harmless superlative in its day; the only thing worth examining is the habit, older and newer than swing, of praising good things in the language of killing.
corruption_paragraphs: Nobody sinned by calling Glenn Miller a killer-diller. The word was play, rhymed for the fun of it. Still, a family can notice a pattern: English slang keeps reaching for kill, slay, and murder to say "wonderful," and words shape how lightly we hold the things they name.

The remedy is not scolding but choosing. Speech that ministers grace (Eph 4:29) has plenty of words for excellence that do not borrow from the sixth commandment (Exo 20:13). And the men who knew war best are often the ones who chose those words most carefully.
roots_summary: English killer (one who kills) → 1930s slang killer (something overwhelming) → rhyming killer-diller (late 1930s swing) → 1940s first-rate thing.
roots_lines: Old English root cwellan, Middle English killen — to kill
1930s American slang: killer — something overwhelmingly good
Late 1930s swing: killer-diller — rhyming intensive
1940s: a hot band, a great record, anything sensational
usage: "Grandpa says the Saturday dance at the Elks was a real killer-diller, and then he went quiet and talked about the boys who didn’t come back."
Death and life are in the power of the tongue (Pro 18:21).
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory (1Co 15:55).

etymology: American slang of the early 1920s, one of a family of nonsense superlatives (the bee’s knees, the cat’s whiskers) from the flapper years, when pajamas were themselves a fashionable novelty. Of no known coiner. It outlived the Jazz Age and was still heard from Silent Generation parents and children in the 1940s and 1950s.
biblical_def: When something was the very best — Mother’s apple pie, a new Schwinn, the girl next door — it was the cat’s pajamas. The phrase made no sense, and that was the fun of it: a cat in pajamas was absurd, so the best things were absurdly good. Your great-grandparents started it in the 1920s and your grandparents kept it going. The Christian question is a simple one: what really is the best? Scripture answers plainly. Paul had been a rising young man with every advantage, and he wrote, "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord" (Php 3:8). Jesus told of a merchant who, "when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it" (Mat 13:46). That pearl is the kingdom of heaven, and Christ is its treasure. David said it this way: "in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore" (Psa 16:11). God does not mind our enjoying the small best things; He made the apples for the pie. But He teaches us to "approve things that are excellent" (Php 1:10) — to rank them rightly. A Schwinn rusts. A pie is gone by Tuesday. The very best thing is not a thing at all; it is Christ, and He does not wear out.
webster_summary: Flapper-era slang kept alive by the Silent Generation (1920s–40s) for the very best, the superb — a playful superlative that asks the serious question of what really is best, answered in the excellency of the knowledge of Christ (Php 3:8).
webster_full: CAT’S PAJAMAS, n. phr. (American slang, 1920s; still common with the Silent Generation, 1940s–50s) The very best; something superb. "Your mother’s pie is the cat’s pajamas." Compare the bee’s knees.
Decode for families: the cat’s pajamas means the best of the best — and it is meant to sound silly.
scriptures: Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
That ye may approve things that are excellent; that ye may be sincere and without offence till the day of Christ;
corruption_summary: A wholesome, silly superlative; the only lesson in it is the question it raises — what is truly the best — which Scripture answers in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct here. The cat’s pajamas is pure fun, the kind of nonsense that children love and grandparents remember fondly. It praises good things, and good things are God’s gifts.

The word does give a family a fine question for the supper table: of all the things we call the best, which will last? Paul counted everything else loss beside Christ (Php 3:8), and that is not a gloomy thought but a happy one — it means the best thing cannot be taken away.
roots_summary: 1920s flapper nonsense superlatives (bee’s knees, cat’s whiskers) → cat’s pajamas (the very best) → kept alive by Silent Generation families, 1940s–50s.
roots_lines: Hindi paijama → English pajamas — loose trousers; sleepwear, a 1920s novelty
Early 1920s: the bee’s knees, the cat’s whiskers — nonsense superlatives
Early 1920s: the cat’s pajamas — the very best
1940s–50s: still current in Silent Generation homes
usage: "Grandma tasted my first loaf of bread and said it was the cat’s pajamas. It was a little burnt."
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy (Psa 16:11).
That ye may approve things that are excellent (Php 1:10).

etymology: From jazz slang gone (carried away by the music, out of this world), recorded by the 1940s, intensified with real. In the 1950s real gone passed from jazz musicians to rock-and-roll teenagers, who used it for a wild song, a great dancer, or a fellow who was simply too much. Of no known coiner.
biblical_def: A real gone record in 1956 was one that carried you clean away — you forgot the homework, the chores, the world. A real gone guy was so caught up in the music he was hardly there. The word confesses something true: people want to be carried out of themselves. God made us that way, and He meant us to be carried away by Him. The world offers cheaper ways to be gone — the bottle, the loud crowd, the thrill. Scripture puts the two side by side: "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit" (Eph 5:18). On the day of Pentecost the mockers thought the apostles were gone the wrong way: "These men are full of new wine" (Act 2:13). They were not; they were full of God. Even Jesus’ own friends once said of Him, "He is beside himself" (Mar 3:21), because His zeal looked like madness. Paul answered such talk: "whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause" (2Co 5:13). The Christian is meant to be wholly taken up with Christ and at the same time clear-headed: "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about" (1Pe 5:8). Lost in a song for three minutes is harmless. Lost to the world because you are found in Christ is the real thing.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1940s jazz, 1950s rock and roll) for carried away by the music, wild, excellent — a word for the human hunger to be taken out of oneself, which Scripture answers not with wine but with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).
webster_full: REAL GONE, adj. phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; from 1940s jazz gone) Carried away by music; wild; excellent. "That record is real gone." "He’s a real gone cat."
Decode for families: real gone meant swept away by the music — the Bible says be swept up in the Spirit, and keep a clear head.
scriptures: And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit;
Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine.
And when his friends heard of it, they went out to lay hold on him: for they said, He is beside himself.
For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause.
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
corruption_summary: Mostly innocent enthusiasm for music; the caution is the deeper hunger it names — to be "gone" — which the world feeds with excess and Scripture fills with the Spirit and sobriety.
corruption_paragraphs: A teenager who called a record real gone meant only that it was great, and there is no harm in being caught up in a good song. The word is worth a second look because of what it praises: being out of oneself, out of control, carried away.

That longing is God-given, but it can be fed the wrong way. The jazz world that coined gone also knew a good deal about drink and worse. Scripture does not tell us to be dull; it tells us where to be carried — filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18) and, at the same time, sober and watchful (1Pe 5:8).
roots_summary: English gone (departed) → 1940s jazz gone (transported by music) → real gone (intensive) → 1950s rock-and-roll teen slang (wild, excellent).
roots_lines: Old English gan → gone — departed, away
1940s jazz slang: gone — carried away by the music
Late 1940s–50s: real gone — the intensive form
1950s rock and roll: real gone — wild, terrific, too much
usage: "When that saxophone took off, the whole gym went real gone — even the chaperones were tapping their feet."
And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit (Eph 5:18).
Be sober, be vigilant (1Pe 5:8).

etymology: A 1950s jazz and beatnik use of most as a stand-alone superlative: something wonderful was simply the most (and something better still, the mostest). Recorded in 1950s slang; of no known coiner. Most itself is an Old English word, the superlative of much and many, and Webster gave its plain senses in 1828.
biblical_def: If your grandfather was a teenager in 1958 and a song was great, he might have said it was the most — no noun, no explanation, just the most. It was the highest praise the slang allowed. But the Bible has its own, much older use of the phrase, and it is a name of God: "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty" (Psa 91:1). There is one Being who really is the most, and everything else is less. That is why His great commandment asks for everything: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind" (Mat 22:37). Jesus added, "This is the first and great commandment" (Mat 22:38). And the Son of God, who is above all, came down to be the least. He told His disciples, who were arguing about which of them would be greatest, "If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all" (Mar 9:35). He did it Himself, all the way to the cross, and God raised Him up, "that in all things he might have the preeminence" (Col 1:18). So when Grandpa says something is the most, you can smile and agree — for a song, that is fine. But keep the real title for the One who holds it.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s jazz and beatnik talk) for the very best, the ultimate — an echo of the Bible’s own name for God, the most High (Psa 91:1), whose Son became servant of all and has the preeminence (Col 1:18).
webster_full: THE MOST, n. phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz and beatnik talk) The very best; the ultimate. "That record is the most." Also the mostest.

Webster (1828) — MOST, adjective superlative of more. 1. Consisting of the greatest number. That scheme of life is to be preferred, which presents a prospect of the most advantages with the fewest inconveniences.
Decode for families: the most meant the best; in the Bible, "the most High" is a name of God.
scriptures: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.
This is the first and great commandment.
And he sat down, and called the twelve, and saith unto them, If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all.
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
corruption_summary: A harmless superlative; its only lesson is about ranking — the true "most" is God, and the way up in His kingdom is down.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in the most needs correcting. It is teenage exaggeration, and a song can be great without anyone sinning. The phrase is worth a moment because exaggeration has a way of using up our words: if a record is the most, what is left to say about God?

Scripture keeps the superlatives for Him — the most High (Psa 91:1), the first and great commandment (Mat 22:38) — and then surprises us: the Most High came to be servant of all (Mar 9:35). A family can enjoy the slang and still teach children that the highest place belongs to Christ alone (Col 1:18).
roots_summary: Old English superlative of much → English most (greatest in amount or degree) → 1950s jazz and beatnik the most (the very best) → the mostest.
roots_lines: Old English — superlative of much, many
1828 Webster: most — greatest in number, quantity, or degree
KJV: the most High — a name of God
1950s jazz and beatnik slang: the most — the very best
Late 1950s: the mostest — playful double superlative
usage: "Grandpa heard his first Fats Domino record in ’56 and told his mother it was the most. She told him to turn it down."
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty (Psa 91:1).
If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all (Mar 9:35).

etymology: From craze (to crack, to shatter), a Middle English word probably of Scandinavian origin; so crazy first meant cracked or full of flaws, then broken in mind, and Webster gave both senses in 1828. Jazz musicians turned it around by the late 1920s to mean exciting, wonderful; by the 1950s the bop and beat crowd said crazy, man, crazy for anything they liked.
biblical_def: In a 1950s coffeehouse, if a fellow played a wild saxophone solo, someone would say, "Crazy, man." It meant great. The older meaning was not great at all: cracked, broken, out of one’s right mind. The slang turned a sorrow into a compliment, and there is a strange truth in that, because the world has always called God’s best things crazy. Paul wrote that "the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God" (1Co 1:18). When Paul preached the resurrection before a Roman governor, Festus shouted, "Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad" (Act 26:24). Paul answered, "I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness" (Act 26:25). The gospel sounds crazy to the world because it is truer than the world. And Christ is the One who heals real madness. The man of the Gadarenes, wild among the tombs, was found "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind" (Mar 5:15). That is what Jesus does: "God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind" (2Ti 1:7). So the Christian should be gentle with the word. Real affliction of the mind is suffering, not a joke, and those who bear it deserve our kindness. And the Christian should not mind being called crazy for Christ.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (jazz from the late 1920s; bop and beat 1950s) for exciting, wonderful — a reversal of the 1828 sense of cracked or deranged, as the world calls the preaching of the cross foolishness (1Co 1:18).
webster_full: CRAZY, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; jazz use from the late 1920s) Excellent, exciting, wonderful. "Crazy, man, crazy!"

Webster (1828) — CRAZY, adjective 1. Broken; decrepit; weak; feeble; applied to the body, or constitution, or any structure; as a crazy body; a crazy constitution; a crazy ship. 2. Broken, weakened, or disordered in intellect; deranged, weakened, or shattered in mind. We say, the man is crazy
Decode for families: in the coffeehouse, crazy meant great; in the Bible, the world calls the gospel crazy, and Christ gives a sound mind.
scriptures: For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God.
And as he thus spake for himself, Festus said with a loud voice, Paul, thou art beside thyself; much learning doth make thee mad.
But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.
And they come to Jesus, and see him that was possessed with the devil, and had the legion, sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid.
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
corruption_summary: The jazz compliment is harmless; the care Scripture asks is not to make light of real affliction of the mind, and not to fear being called crazy for the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Crazy as praise did no harm in 1955 and does none now. The word does carry an older weight. For most of its history it named a real and painful thing, and children should learn not to mock anyone who suffers in mind. Christ met such sufferers with compassion and healing (Mar 5:15), and so should His people.

The other lesson runs the opposite way. The world has always judged the gospel to be madness (1Co 1:18; Act 26:24). A Christian should expect it, answer with "truth and soberness" as Paul did, and not be ashamed.
roots_summary: Middle English crasen (to crack, shatter) → crazy (cracked; deranged) → late-1920s jazz (exciting, wonderful) → 1950s bop and beat crazy, man.
roots_lines: Middle English crasen — to break, to crack; probably Scandinavian
16th c.–: crazy — cracked, full of flaws; then broken in mind
Late 1920s jazz: crazy — exciting, wonderful
1950s bop and beat: crazy, man, crazy — general praise
usage: "Uncle Bill played one chord on the coffeehouse piano and a bearded fellow said, ‘Crazy.’ Uncle Bill thought he was being insulted."
For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind (2Ti 1:7).
I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness (Act 26:25).

etymology: The word gas was coined in the 1600s by the Flemish chemist J. B. van Helmont, from Greek chaos, and Webster defined it as an aeriform fluid in 1828. American slang used gas for empty talk by the mid-1800s. The sense of great fun, a thrill ("what a gas!"), grew up in jazz and teen talk and was common by the 1950s and 1960s.
biblical_def: When a hayride or a sock hop was great fun, a teenager of 1959 said, "What a gas!" It was a happy word, and fun is not a sin. God gave His people feasts and laughter. When He brought them home from captivity, "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing" (Psa 126:2). Solomon wrote, "A merry heart doeth good like a medicine" (Pro 17:22), and Nehemiah told the people to eat and drink and rejoice, "for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). A Christian home ought to be the merriest house on the block. But gas has an older slang meaning too: hot air, empty talk. Job’s friend asked, "Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind?" (Job 15:2). Fun chased for its own sake turns out to be gas in that sense — it fills you up and leaves nothing behind. Solomon tried that road and reported, "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2). The joy that lasts is the joy of the LORD — joy in a Savior who forgave our sins and will raise us up. Christians are the people who can enjoy a hayride most, because the hayride is not all they have.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s–60s; "what a gas!") for great fun, a thrill — a cheerful word with an older slang twin meaning empty talk, a reminder that only the joy of the LORD is strength (Neh 8:10).
webster_full: GAS, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s–60s; jazz and teen talk) Great fun; a thrill; something delightful. "The hayride was a gas!" Older slang: empty talk, hot air.
Webster (1828) — GAS, noun In chimistry, a permanently elastic aeriform fluid, or a substance reduced to the state of an aeriform fluid by its permanent combination with caloric.
Decode for families: a gas is a good time; all gas is hot air — the joy of the Lord is the real thing.
scriptures: Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing: then said they among the heathen, The LORD hath done great things for them.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Should a wise man utter vain knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind?
I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?
corruption_summary: A wholesome word for fun; the only caution is the emptiness of fun pursued for its own sake, which Solomon tested and found to be wind.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with calling a good time a gas. Scripture is full of feasting, singing, and laughter, and a merry heart is good medicine (Pro 17:22). Grandparents who used the word were usually describing exactly the kind of clean fun a family should want more of.

The older slang sense is a fair warning, though. Fun that has nothing beneath it is hot air — the east wind Job’s friend mentioned (Job 15:2). Solomon chased pleasure as far as a man can and found it could not answer "What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2). The joy that holds is the joy of the LORD (Neh 8:10).
roots_summary: Greek chaos → Flemish chemist’s gas (1600s) → English gas (aeriform fluid) → 1800s slang (empty talk) → 1950s–60s a gas (great fun).
roots_lines: Greek chaos — empty space, formless matter
1600s: gas coined by J. B. van Helmont for an airlike substance
1828 Webster: gas — an aeriform fluid
Mid-1800s American slang: gas — empty, boastful talk
1950s–60s jazz and teen slang: a gas — great fun, a thrill
usage: "Grandma says the church hayride of ’58 was a gas — right up until the wagon tipped into the creek."
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine (Pro 17:22).
Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing (Psa 126:2).

etymology: Of uncertain origin. Jazz musicians used gig for a paid engagement, especially a single night’s job, from the 1920s; by the 1940s and 1950s every working musician lived on gigs, and later any job at all could be a gig. The older English gig — a whirling toy, a light two-wheeled carriage, a ship’s boat — is the word Webster recorded in 1828; no link between it and the musicians’ sense is proven.
biblical_def: To a dance-band trumpeter in 1948, a gig was a job — Saturday night at the Elks hall, twelve dollars and supper. Musicians lived gig to gig. The word has spread, and your generation uses it for any job, especially a short one. The Bible honours the working musician. Young David’s first job at the palace was a gig of sorts: when Saul was troubled, "David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well" (1Sa 16:23). The psalm says to "play skilfully with a loud noise" (Psa 33:3) — skill is a way of honouring God. And the musician deserves his pay like any worker: "the labourer is worthy of his hire" (Luk 10:7). The danger in a gig is the attitude that can come with it — it is only a gig, only for tonight, not worth my best. Scripture shuts that door: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23), and "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might" (Ecc 9:10). A Christian plays the Elks hall as if the Lord were in the front row, because He is. And the best news for a man living gig to gig is that his life is not a string of gigs. In Christ he has a calling, a Master who never lays him off, and a reward that does not run out.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (jazz from the 1920s; common 1940s–50s) for a musician’s paid engagement, later any job — work Scripture honours when it is done heartily, as to the Lord (Col 3:23), with the labourer worthy of his hire.
webster_full: GIG, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; jazz musicians’ word from the 1920s) A paid engagement for a musician, especially one night’s job; later, any job. "We’ve got a gig at the Legion hall Saturday."
Webster (1828) — GIG, noun 1. Any little thing that is whirled round in play. 2. A light carriage with one pair of wheels, drawn by one horse; a chair or chaise. 3. A fiddle.
Decode for families: a gig is a job, often a short one — but a Christian works every one of them for the Lord.
scriptures: And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
corruption_summary: An honest working word; the only snare is the half-hearted attitude that treats a short job as not worth one’s best, which Scripture answers with work done heartily as to the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Gig is a plain word for honest work, and nothing in it needs correcting. Musicians who played weddings, dances, and church suppers through the 1940s and 1950s were laborers worthy of their hire (Luk 10:7), and many of them were faithful men.

The word can carry an attitude, though: a gig is temporary, so why give it everything? Scripture answers that every job, long or short, is done before the Lord (Col 3:23; Ecc 9:10). There are no small gigs when the Master is watching.
roots_summary: English gig (whirling toy; light carriage; ship’s boat, by 1828) — separate, uncertain → 1920s jazz gig (a paid engagement) → 1940s–50s working musicians’ word → any job.
roots_lines: Middle English gigge — a whirling thing; origin uncertain
1828 Webster: gig — a top; a light carriage; a ship’s boat
1920s jazz: gig — a paid engagement, one night’s job
1940s–50s: the working musician’s everyday word
Later: gig — any job, especially a short one
usage: "Grandpa’s trio had a gig every Saturday at the Grange hall — three dollars apiece and all the pie they could eat."
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men (Col 3:23).
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might (Ecc 9:10).

etymology: American, recorded by the early 1940s; zoot is generally taken as a rhyming play on suit, and no coiner is known. The suit had a long, wide-shouldered coat reaching nearly to the knees and high-waisted trousers, full at the knee and pegged tight at the ankle, often worn with a long watch chain and a broad hat. Popular with swing fans around 1940–42, it ran into wartime cloth rationing in 1942, when federal regulations limited the fabric in men’s clothing and the extravagant suit came to look wasteful.
biblical_def: In 1942 a young man in a zoot suit could be seen a block away: a coat to his knees, shoulders out to here, trousers billowing at the knee and tight at the ankle, a watch chain swinging nearly to the sidewalk. It was a way of saying, Look at me. Then the war came, cloth was rationed, and most boys traded the zoot suit for a uniform. Scripture is not against good clothes; God Himself dresses the lilies, and Jesus said "even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these" (Mat 6:29). But it warns against loving the look more than the man inside it. "Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning" (1Pe 3:3), says Peter; "let it be the hidden man of the heart" (1Pe 3:4) — the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit. And God reminded Samuel that "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The finest suit any man will ever wear is not cut by a tailor: "he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness" (Isa 61:10). Everyone baptized into Christ has "put on Christ" (Gal 3:27). That suit never goes out of style, it was paid for at the cross, and when people look at the man who wears it, they are meant to see Him.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (early 1940s) for the exaggerated, wide-shouldered, long-coated suit of the swing era — a garment that said "look at me," where Scripture prizes the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4) and the robe of righteousness.
webster_full: ZOOT SUIT, n. (Silent Generation slang, early 1940s; swing era) A flamboyant men’s suit with a long, wide-shouldered coat and high-waisted, pegged trousers, often with a long watch chain. "He showed up at the dance in a zoot suit and a hat as wide as a wagon wheel."
Decode for families: the zoot suit was the loudest outfit of 1942 — the Bible says the best clothing is the robe of righteousness Christ gives.
scriptures: And yet I say unto you, That even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these.
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.

I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels.
For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
corruption_summary: A fashion word, not a sinful one; the caution it carries is vanity — loving the look more than the heart, and spending lavishly on display.
corruption_paragraphs: The zoot suit was youthful flash, and most of the young men who wore one were simply having their moment, the way every generation does. A suit is not a sin, and Scripture does not ask anyone to dress drab.

The lesson is the old one about vanity. Clothes that exist to say "look at me" turn the eyes toward the wearer rather than toward God, and in a year of rationing they also looked careless of others. Peter’s word stands: the ornament worth having is the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4), and the robe worth wearing is the one Christ gives (Isa 61:10).
roots_summary: English suit (a matched set of clothes) → rhyming zoot suit (early 1940s swing fashion) → checked by 1942 wartime cloth rationing → a byword for flamboyant dress.
roots_lines: French suite → English suit — a matched set of clothes
Around 1940–42: zoot suit — rhyming name for the exaggerated swing suit
1942: wartime cloth rationing curbs the style
Later: zoot suit — a byword for loud, flamboyant clothing
usage: "Great-Uncle Ray saved up for a zoot suit in ’41, wore it twice, and then wore khaki for four years."
But let it be the hidden man of the heart (1Pe 3:4).
For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ (Gal 3:27).
